title: The Picture He Built Alone
description:
Three nights. A registry record, a line from an article a dozen years old, one remembered scene at a time.

The name he steered away from — Han PD Construction. The 'Im' who vouched for Park Sang-jin to his father. The man who came up from a Chungcheong fishing town and reached Gangnam by stepping on people.

Three threads met at one point. Im Sangchul.

No one told him. Minjun built the man out of fragments.
And once he knew, the same seat in the same café looked different.

choices.text: Hold the cards — knowing is its own power
choices.result_text:
Minjun closed the notebook.

He wouldn't tear the man down, wouldn't forgive him either. He would simply know.
He'd sit at the same table knowing exactly who this man was.

This time, the one holding the cards was Minjun.

choices.text: See the man again — one day I'll ask him directly
choices.result_text:
Minjun looked at the Gangnam lights for a long time.

He wanted to ask. Why did you do it. Knowing, why did you let me in.

Not yet. But the question was inside him now, clear and waiting.

choices.text: Swallow it — Gangnam comes first for now
choices.result_text:
He wouldn't let on that he knew. He'd set the next meeting like nothing happened.

Someday this weight would come back around.
Until then — Gangnam first.

Minjun turned off the light. Sleep didn't come.

title: A Name That Stayed
description:
There was a name Sangchul had quietly steered away from at the network dinner. "Han PD Construction."
Minjun filed it away in the back of his mind. Weeks passed.

Tonight, he couldn't sleep. He searched the name.
An old article. A real estate guarantee scam. A broker who made the introductions. The name was redacted — but the timing, the district, the pattern — it all mirrored what happened to his father.

And at the bottom of the article, in the list of related entities: Han PD Construction.
The same name Sangchul's face hadn't changed at all while he deflected.

choices.text: Dig deeper — trace Sangchul's old transactions
choices.result_text:
Registry records. Old articles. Corporate histories. He dug through all of it until dawn.

The pieces aligned. Same window. Same neighborhood. Same referral structure.

Lim. Sang. Chul.

Minjun's father never spoke the name. Minjun had found it himself.
The man who'd been teaching him to read charts — the same man who years ago walked his father into financial ruin.

No one told him. He figured it out alone.
That weight was heavier.

choices.text: Leave it alone — he can't be sure
choices.result_text:
You can't accuse someone based on one article.
Minjun closed his laptop.

But — a suspicion, once caught, doesn't let go easily.
Every time he saw Sangchul now, that name rang somewhere quiet inside him.

He'd pretend not to know. For now.

title: Father's Secret
description:
After the hospital visit, Dad started calling more often.
Short calls. How's the weather. Have you eaten.

Today was different.
He spoke slowly.
"Minjun. About that debt. It was... Park Sang-jin."

Minjun had never heard that name before.

"Someone from the Gangnam real estate scene introduced us. A man named Im. He seemed decent at first... He said Park Sang-jin was someone you could trust."

Minjun set down the cup he'd been holding.

Today was different.
He spoke slowly.
"Minjun. That debt. It was Park Sang-jin. A man named Im introduced us."

Minjun already knew.
He'd pieced it together alone — in the small hours, from old articles and registry records.
Im Sangchul.

Hearing it from his father's mouth was different.
The weight he'd been carrying alone — now it belonged to both of them.

Minjun set his cup down slowly.

choices.text: "That man named Im — do you happen to know his full name?"

"Im... Sangchul, I think he said. Why?"

Lim. Sang. Chul.

The broker who ruined his father years ago. That man is Minjun's mentor right now. The one who sits across from him at the same café, teaching him how to read charts.

The hand holding the phone went cold.

choices.text: "Do you know where he is now?"
choices.result_text:
"No idea. Somewhere in Gangnam, I suppose."

Minjun knows.

Not just somewhere in Gangnam — Im Sangchul still sits at the same table in the same café. Teaching Minjun how to trade charts.

Dad doesn't know. He has no idea that man has walked right into the middle of his son's life.

choices.result_text:
After a long silence, Dad spoke again.
"I just... felt like I had to tell you. I'm sorry, son."

Minjun couldn't even say "it's okay." He ended the call.
And sat alone in his room.

Im Sangchul.

title: Mirror
description:
Late at night, Sangchul spoke.

"Minjun, can I be honest with you?"

{name} set down his glass.

"At first I just thought you were someone with drive.
But the more I watch you — you're like me.
You know how to move fast.
You know what you have to let go of."

{name} said nothing.

"I don't mean that as an insult. It's a compliment."

Through the window, Gangnam glittered.

title: The Question
description:
For a month, Minjun did nothing.
He still met Sangchul. Talked like usual. Charts, markets, strategy for next month.

Then today, he reached his limit.

He set his coffee down and spoke.
"Sangchul. Do you know a man named Park Sang-jin?"

choices.text: Waited for Sangchul's reaction
choices.result_text:
Sangchul's hand stopped.

He didn't deny it. He didn't pretend to be surprised.
He just — went quiet for a moment.

"...How did you find out?"

choices.text: "Forget it." (He took it back)
choices.result_text:
Something shifted in Sangchul's eyes the instant Minjun took the words back.

He didn't say, "All right." He didn't say, "I don't know him."

It was the face of a man who already knew how much Minjun knew.

choices.text: (He got up and left)
choices.result_text:

Sangchul called his name from across the café.

Minjun pushed through the glass door. He hadn't looked back — not yet.

title: Cold Coffee
description:
The hiss of the espresso machine returned when Minjun took the question back. The café resumed around them as though nothing had happened.

Instead of answering, Sangchul pushed the water glass toward him. One finger traced the brown ring on the saucer.

"If you're going to stay beside me, you should know what pretending not to know will cost."

"What cost?" Minjun asked.

"Whether you use me later or throw me away — you chose not to ask today. That cost."

He didn't press for an answer. That was how Minjun knew: this silence was no longer ignorance. It was a contract.

choices.text: "I'll leave it buried."
choices.result_text:
Minjun drank the water. It tasted of less than the cold coffee.

I still need what this man knows, he told himself exactly three times. That was all.

When Minjun stood first, Sangchul didn't stop him. One name remained on the table, known to both men and spoken by neither.

choices.text: "No. Tell me all of it."
choices.result_text:
Minjun pushed the water glass back across the table.

"Then I'll hear the cost too. How did you know Park Sang-jin? Start at the beginning."

Sangchul's finger stopped on the saucer. The man who had spent years avoiding this finally settled back into his chair.

title: Outside the Door
description:
The café music thinned behind the closing glass door. Minjun took the three front steps at once. Cold air sharpened the bitterness in his mouth.

"Minjun."

Sangchul didn't follow. He stood inside the threshold, holding the door with one hand.

"If you leave now, you aren't leaving without knowing. You're choosing not to hear it."

Minjun stopped at the foot of the steps. Without turning, he could feel the exact distance between them. Three paces.

choices.text: He never looked back
choices.result_text:
Minjun took the fourth step. Behind him, the glass door closed.

After that day, he never contacted Sangchul first. The information, the introductions, every door Sangchul opened — all of them closed with him.

The relationship ended without a dramatic scene. Only those three steps stayed with Minjun for a long time.

choices.text: He turned at the foot of the steps
choices.result_text:
When Minjun turned, Sangchul was still holding the door.

"I'll hear everything before I go."

They returned to the same table. The coffee was stone cold, and this time neither man ordered another cup.

title: I'm Sorry
description:
After a long pause, Lim Sangchul spoke.
"Your father. I knew you were his son from the start."

{name} didn't answer. He only looked at his coffee cup. The steam had long gone cold.

"You're the one who introduced Park Sang-jin to him, weren't you?"

Sangchul nodded. "I told him Park could be trusted. I vouched for him. I thought I was doing one favor. I didn't know it would become this." It didn't sound like an excuse. That made it harder to bear.

Silence again. Then Sangchul said, "I'm sorry."

Those words, carried across more than a decade, were laid on the table. {name} couldn't pick them up right away.

choices.text: "I'm going to report you."
choices.result_text:
"I'm going to report you." {name}'s voice didn't shake.
Sangchul nodded quietly. "...Right. I think that's what's correct." No surprise, no plea.

{name} rose. In that moment the network was severed. Sangchul's information, his doors, his people — all gone with it. Gangnam receded that far again.
And yet, strangely, his feet were light going down the stairs. Between what he'd lost and what he'd taken back, which was larger, {name} could not yet reckon.

choices.text: "That's all I needed to hear." (He let it go)
choices.result_text:
"That one word was enough," {name} said.
Sangchul lifted his head and looked at him. "...Thank you."

Being thanked felt strange. He was thanking the one who had apologized.
And still — maybe this was the right way. Tearing it all open, breaking it all down, wouldn't bring Father back. Setting down the hatred wasn't the same as forgiveness. {name} had simply decided to set down one weight.

choices.text: "I'm only here because of you." (He chose to use it)
choices.result_text:
"It's thanks to you that I'm even here." When {name} said it, Sangchul paused.
"...So that's how you'll use it."

{name} smiled. The smile felt strange even to himself.
This man had ruined his father. And yet without this man's network, he couldn't reach Gangnam. So he folded the hatred away and chose to use this hand as a tool.
The math was right. Only, after that day, it grew a little harder to look his own face straight in the mirror.

choices.text: "Pay it back. My father's debt. With your own hands."
choices.result_text:
"Pay it back. My father's debt. With your own hands." {name} said it, clear and even.
Sangchul looked at him a long time. "...So that's what you want."
"An apology doesn't fill my father's bankbook."

Instead of answering, Sangchul took out a notebook. A few days later, money entered Father's old account. The sum that had vanished over a decade ago returned, exact to the number.
And yet even as he confirmed that number, something in {name} stayed unfilled. The debt was paid — but the decade Father had lost did not come back.

title: The Same Question
description:
A message came from Jaehyuk.
It had been a while. Contact had gone thin since the scam arc.

"Minjun. I've got an investment deal going — could you co-sign a guarantee, just once?"

{name} set the phone down and looked out the window a long time.
A guarantee. Those words.

That was exactly how Father had been ruined. Someone's favor, one signature he couldn't refuse. {name} knew that in that seat now sat not his father, but himself.

choices.text: "No." (He refused, flat)
choices.result_text:
"I can't." {name} kept it short. Say more, and he might waver.
A silence. Jaehyuk answered, "...Okay." That was all. No anger, no resentment. Which made it linger longer.

{name} set the phone on the table and thought of his father.
Father must have had this moment too. Before a friend's request, the moment when refusing felt like being a bad person. Father couldn't refuse; {name} did.
To make a different choice in the same seat — maybe that was all {name} had learned in five years.

choices.text: "How much are we talking?" (He decided to hear it out)
choices.result_text:
"How much is it?" {name} decided to at least hear it out.
Jaehyuk explained. The whole time, an odd feeling wouldn't leave. Was this man hiding something again? Or — was it really a good deal this time? He couldn't tell.

In the end, {name} signed. Refusing to trust an old friend felt like its own kind of wrong.
The moment he signed, his father's face flickered past. Father must have felt exactly this — not a hand held out from failing to doubt, but from wanting to believe.

choices.text: (He closed the message and pretended not to have seen it)
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the message as if he hadn't read it, and opened another app.
A practical choice. He didn't want to get tangled with Jaehyuk further. Look away just this once, and it would pass quietly.

But on the day Father signed his guarantee too, this man must have reached out just like this. Bright, urgent, familiar.
{name} looked at the dark phone screen a moment. Looking away and refusing were not the same thing. Which was more of a coward's move, he couldn't quite say.

title: Three Times Absent
description:
The hospital called.
His father was in critical condition, they said. He had to come down at once.
"Are you able to come down right now?"

It wasn't the first such call Minjun had taken.
Three times. All three, he hadn't gone down. Something important came up. A deal came up. No time. Each time he told himself so, and each time it sounded reasonable enough.

This call was — the fourth.
The nurse's voice on the other end was different from the three before. Not urgent. A voice for which there was no longer any need to hurry.
Phone in hand, Minjun couldn't move for a long while.

title: Before Departure
description:
Seoul Station on a winter night. Dry heated air leaked through the open train door. The departure board and the deal alert on his phone showed the same minute.

"This train will depart shortly. Please board now."

Minjun stood before the door. The phone in his pocket rang once more, then stopped. The hospital number.

The train door and the stairs lay in opposite directions. Neither had closed yet.

choices.text: (He took the KTX. Knowing he was already too late.)

text_if_moral.black: (Take the KTX. Move before he finishes calculating the loss.)
text_if_moral.white: (Take the KTX. Even if it is too late, go where he needs to be.)

choices.result_text: The KTX felt impossibly slow. The whole way, as the scenery fled backward outside the window, Minjun tried to think of nothing at all.

choices.text: Turn back before the doors close. Take the deal.

text_if_moral.black: Turn away from the train. This deal disappears if he waits.
text_if_moral.white: Turn away from the train. Take the deal, knowing what he is leaving behind.

choices.result_text:
"I'm sorry. This time I really can't come." Minjun called the hospital back and said it. Then he went into the deal.
He made five million won on it. Just as planned.

title: Ten Minutes
description:
A contract and a bottle of water gone warm sat in the meeting room. The person across from Minjun checked the time.

"We need your signature within ten minutes. The other side is waiting too."

Minjun's phone lay face down on the table. Each vibration made the thin glass surface hum. Turn it over: the hospital number. Turn it back: the signature line.

His pen would not settle in his hand. Seoul Station was twelve minutes away by taxi.

choices.text: Put down the pen. Take the fastest KTX.

text_if_moral.black: Put down the pen. Leave before the calculation is complete.
text_if_moral.white: Put down the pen. Go where he needs to be before it is any later.

choices.result_text:
Minjun stood, leaving the signature line blank. Someone called his name, but he did not turn around.

The KTX felt impossibly slow. The whole way, as the scenery fled backward outside the window, Minjun tried to think of nothing at all.

choices.text: (He hung up. There was a deal he had to close right now.)

text_if_moral.black: (Hang up. This deal vanishes if he does not take it now.)
text_if_moral.white: (Hang up. Take the deal, knowing what he is leaving behind.)

choices.result_text:
"I'm sorry. This time I really can't come." Minjun hung up. And he went into the deal.
He made five million won on it. Just as planned.

title: One Hour
description:
By the time he reached Changwon Station, Father was already gone.
The nurse said, "An hour ago." Exactly one hour.

The door to the room stood open. The sheet had been pulled tight again and the bedside cabinet was bare. The traces of someone having been removed were clearer than the traces of anyone having stayed.

choices.text: Sit beside the empty bed.
choices.result_text:
Minjun sat beside the empty hospital bed. He stayed like that a long time. Nothing was left but the smell of antiseptic.
He'd wanted to show him. That the number in the bankbook had climbed this high, that his son had made it this far — and now there was one fewer person in the world to show it to.
In his pocket, the phone still held a call log from some day long ago. Twenty-three seconds.

title: Five Million Won
description:
The next morning, another call came in the empty meeting room.

"Your father passed away last night."

At the very hour Minjun was making his five million. The contract had been cleared away, but the deposit alert was still on his screen. After the call ended, the number and the hospital call remained side by side.

choices.text: Open the banking app.
choices.result_text:
Minjun set the phone down and opened the banking app. The number had gone up. Five million won, exactly.
He looked at it a long time. He'd thought he'd feel nothing; he was wrong. That this number would, for the rest of his life, be priced at the same value as this morning — only now did Minjun understand it.

title: Father Comes to Seoul
description:
A message from Father: he's coming to Seoul.

"I'm not trying to bother you. Just want to see your face for a bit. This weekend."

That weekend. A critical investment timing — a decision that had to be made within days.

{name} set down the phone.

Time to see Father — if he wanted to make it, he could. The question was whether he wanted to.

choices.text: Made the time. Ate together.
choices.result_text:
They had a meal. Sat for a long time.

The investment timing passed. No gains that week.
Instead — Father said "Well done, Minjun" on his way out.

That stayed with {name} all week.

choices.text: Said let's meet next time. The timing isn't right.
choices.result_text:
The investment worked out. Money came in.

Father said "Alright, let's meet later."

That voice lingered for a moment after the call ended.
{name} just opened the next chart.

choices.text: Met briefly at the station. Just an hour.
choices.result_text:
Coffee in Seoul Station's waiting area.
One hour.

Father said "You must be busy." {name} said "No, not really."

Watched him get on the subway. Wished they'd stayed a little longer.

title: The Weight of 1 billion won
description:
Portfolio and cash combined crossed 1 billion won.

{name} looked at the number for a long time.

Wanted to tell someone. But — wasn't sure who that number could be shared with.

Not bragging. Just wanting to share that something had changed.
But there was no one nearby who would understand what had changed.

This is what loneliness feels like, {name} thought.

choices.text: Just went to sleep. A number only {name} knows.
choices.result_text:
Turned off the light.

One billion won. A number only {name} knows.

Tomorrow the charts open again, and this feeling will disappear.
No — not disappear. Somewhere it accumulates.

choices.text: Wanted to call Father. Even if not about the number.
choices.result_text:
Father picked up.
"Oh, Minjun."

Didn't say the number. Talked about food, weather.

After hanging up, the loneliness of 1 billion won felt a little lighter.
You don't have to share the number for something to be shared.

choices.text: Strangely lonely that no one would understand this number
choices.result_text:
Lonely. Honestly.

Still far from Gangnam — a third of the way there.
But having come this far without building anyone to celebrate with — that was the shadow this number cast.

title: The Last Week
description:
Seven days until the 38th birthday.

Five years ending.

Whether the goal was reached or not — five years passed anyway.
The person with 500,000 won in the bank made it here.

{name} looked at who they'd become and thought:

If the person from five years ago saw who this is now — what would they say?

choices.text: "You did well." Even if it wasn't enough.
choices.result_text:
The person from five years ago — didn't know getting this far was possible.

Regardless of whether the goal was reached, getting here was something that person never expected.

"Good job." {name} said it inwardly, to himself.
No one heard it. Still needed to be said.

choices.text: "Is this all?" Could have done better.
choices.result_text:
Not wrong. There were moments that could have been seized better.

But if every one of those moments had been seized — would this be the same person?

{name} didn't know the answer.
Probably still wouldn't know five more years from now.

choices.text: "I'm glad you didn't give up here."
choices.result_text:
Five years ago, there were moments of wanting to quit in that goshiwon room.

Every moment needed a reason. Sometimes there wasn't one. Kept going anyway.

"I'm glad you didn't give up here."

Those words were also something the current {name} needed.

He bet everything on the last hand — and won.

title: Why Gangnam
description:
Eleven at night.

For the first time, his assets had crossed that number.
{name} stood alone where he could see the lights in the direction of Gangnam.

Someone asked.
It might have been his father, Hyunsu, or simply a voice carried from somewhere else.

"Why was it Gangnam in the first place?"

After nearly three years of running, {name} had an answer different from the one he would have given at the start.

description_if_moral.black:
Eleven at night.

For the first time, his assets had crossed that number.
Before looking toward the lights of Gangnam, {name} reopened the account alert. The number had not changed. He refreshed it once more.

Someone asked.
It might have been his father, Hyunsu, or simply a voice carried from somewhere else.

"Why was it Gangnam in the first place?"

The next target came to mind before an answer did. What had changed in three years was less the reason than the speed of his calculation.
description_if_moral.white:
Eleven at night.

For the first time, his assets had crossed that number.
{name} stood alone where he could see the lights in the direction of Gangnam. Below them were people waiting for the last bus and shops whose owners had not yet gone home.

Someone asked.
It might have been his father, Hyunsu, or simply a voice carried from somewhere else. Every voice had a face.

"Why was it Gangnam in the first place?"

For the first time, the answer arrived with names instead of a number.

choices.text: "To prove that I wasn't wrong."

text_if_moral.black: "To prove it. So no one can dismiss me again."
text_if_moral.white: "To prove that I did not break."

choices.result_text:
That was the most honest answer.
To someone — or perhaps to nothing at all — he had wanted to say, 'I wasn't wrong.'

There was nothing wrong with wanting to prove yourself.
{name} simply could not yet say exactly who that proof was for.

choices.text: "I think I wanted to pay back my father's debt — my way."

text_if_moral.black: "To replace what my father lost with a number of my own."
text_if_moral.white: "I think I wanted to pay back my father's debt — my way."

choices.result_text:
Something loosened when he said it to himself.

It was not about paying the money back. His father had lost to the world, and {name} had wanted to repay that by standing before the world again.

Gangnam was the proof. Not a point on a map, but the person standing there.

choices.text: "I thought Gangnam would make things different. Now I'm not sure."

text_if_moral.black: "I thought Gangnam would end it. But the number has not ended anything."
text_if_moral.white: "I thought Gangnam would make things different. Now I'm not sure."

choices.result_text:
It was the most honest answer.

At first, Gangnam had felt like freedom.
Now he could no longer say exactly what it was.

Knowing that he did not know might itself be something he had learned in three years.

description_if_known.motive_clarified:
Eleven at night.

For the first time, his assets had crossed that number.
{name} stood alone where he could see the lights in the direction of Gangnam.

Someone asked.
It might have been his father, Hyunsu, or simply a voice carried from somewhere else.

"Why was it Gangnam in the first place?"

After nearly three years of running, {name} had an answer different from the one he would have given at the start.

He had asked himself this question once before.
On a day when pride and purpose had blurred together, he had sorted through his reasons.
So this time, the answer came at once.

title: KTX, Outside the Window
description:
On the KTX. Outside the window, the scenery slid backward without a sound.
{name} opened the call log. Father. Twenty-three seconds.

No matter how far he scrolled up, that was the first and nearly the only record. In five years, the calls between father and son came to just those few. Twenty-three seconds — what could you fit inside that? No — even in those twenty-three seconds, {name} had wanted to hang up quickly.

His finger stopped over the number. That this train going down might be the last one — he knew it, and was pretending not to.

choices.text: Call him
choices.result_text:
{name} pressed the number.
It rang. Once, twice, three times. No answer.
Maybe, right now, Father was in no state to take a call. The thought turned his fingertips cold.
{name} set the phone down and looked out the window. The scenery kept fleeing backward — at a speed there was no catching.

choices.text: Do not call
choices.result_text:
{name} couldn't bring himself to call. What to say, what to lead with in twenty-three seconds — he didn't know.
The screen went dark on its own. In the black glass, his own face was faintly reflected.
{name} closed his eyes. With them shut, he listened to the scenery fleeing backward and backward. The train still had a long way left to go.
